implementation_notes: Vapor supplies the framework roles: a type conforming to Middleware (or AsyncMiddleware for async/await) receives the Request and a Responder for the remainder of the chain, and returns either the response produced by next.respond(to:) or one it generated itself (short-circuit); registration is app.middleware.use(m) globally or app.grouped(m) per route group, with an explicit at: .beginning option when a middleware must precede the defaults. Order is part of the contract and documented as A -> B -> C -> handler -> C -> B -> A. The classic Interceptor/Dispatcher/Context trio is replaced by the responder chain plus Request/Response; outside Vapor, Foundation's URLProtocol subclasses are the nearest equivalent for intercepting URLSession traffic.
pitfalls: Middleware registered with app.middleware.use lives for the application's lifetime and is shared across event loops: per-request state belongs in request storage, and a middleware registered inside a route handler leaks.

Throwing from a middleware jumps straight to the error middleware, so error handling must be positioned correctly (Vapor's CORSMiddleware must run before ErrorMiddleware, otherwise error responses lack CORS headers).
Positional ordering: adding one middleware at .beginning changes which middleware sees the request first, and route-group middleware always runs after application middleware.
Blocking work inside an async middleware (sync file I/O, blocking network calls) occupies the event loop; use the async APIs or run it off-loop.
